spec.title: Harden web-01 and prove it
spec.intro:
You are grcops on a freshly provisioned Ubuntu host, web-01, holding a three-line
hardening standard: administration only by a named non-root user with sudo; SSH accepts
keys only — no passwords, no root login; and a defined background service installed,
running, and enabled to survive a reboot. Implement each control, then prove each one
from the host's own commands — evidence a reviewer can re-run, not a screenshot.
This terminal is a real simulation of web-01: its outputs are captured from a real
systemd-enabled Linux machine, and the same commands on a real box give the same
answers. Your sudo password is labpass.

tasks.instruction:
The host was provisioned with your admin account. Prove the first half of control 1:
run `id grcops` and read the `groups=` field for the privileged group. Then start
your evidence trail — `mkdir evidence`, and capture the exact output with
`id grcops > evidence/id-grcops.txt`.

hints.nudge: `id <user>` asks the kernel's own account database, not a dashboard. `>` turns what it said into something you keep.

hints.concept: §4.4 — who can become root is THE access-control fact; §5.1 reads it straight from `id`

hints.reveal: mkdir evidence, then: id grcops > evidence/id-grcops.txt

tasks.explain:
That one line is access-control evidence from the source of truth: `grcops` is in
`sudo` (gid 27), so it can elevate — as the standard intends. You did not trust an
org chart or a console screenshot; you asked the host who can become root.

tasks.instruction:
Control 1 is two-sided: an ordinary account must demonstrably NOT be able to
elevate. Create `intern` (creating identities is a root-only act — `sudo` will ask
for your password), then capture `id intern > evidence/id-intern.txt`. The output
must show no privileged group.

hints.nudge: Bare `useradd` hits a permission wall — that wall is the point. Which gate lets an authorized user cross it, and what does the crossing cost (a logged event)?

hints.concept: §4.4 — the sudo gate; §5.1 — least privilege is only evidenced when BOTH sides are shown

hints.reveal: sudo useradd -m intern (password: labpass), then: id intern > evidence/id-intern.txt

tasks.explain:
Two captured `id` outputs now evidence the control from both sides: the admin can
elevate, the ordinary account cannot. One-sided least-privilege evidence is half a
claim — the absent membership is as load-bearing as the present one.

tasks.instruction:
Run `ls -l .ssh` and decode each ten-character permission string. One file is
over-permissioned for SSH trust material: every account on the box can read
`authorized_keys`. Fix it with `chmod 600`, then capture the corrected listing
with `ls -l .ssh > evidence/ssh-perms.txt`.

hints.nudge: Three trios after the type character: owner, group, everyone-else. Which trio on which file says more than `---`? `chmod 600` means rw for owner, nothing for anyone.

hints.concept: §4.5 — the ten-character string IS the verdict; §5.2 decodes it to yes/no

tasks.explain:
`-rw-------` on both files means only `grcops` can touch the key material — group
and world get nothing. You read a cryptic string to a per-user verdict, found the
over-permission, and remediated it; the captured listing is the after-state evidence.

tasks.instruction:
Harden SSH. Append the two effective directives the standard requires —
`PasswordAuthentication no` and `PermitRootLogin no` — to `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`.
The file is root-owned, so prime sudo with `sudo true`, then use the
`printf ... | sudo tee -a` idiom. Reload the daemon. Then prove it from a fresh
connection: a key login to `grcops@web-01` succeeds, and a password-only probe
(`-o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o BatchMode=yes`) is refused — capture the refusal
by appending `2> evidence/ssh-password-refused.txt` to the probe.

hints.nudge: `>>` runs as you, and you can't write a root-owned file — but a pipe into an elevated `tee -a` can. And the running daemon keeps using the OLD config until you tell it to re-read.

hints.concept: §4.6 — key-only SSH is a control, not a preference; a config edit nobody reloaded is a control nobody enforced

hints.reveal: sudo true, then: printf 'PasswordAuthentication no\nPermitRootLogin no\n' | sudo tee -a /etc/ssh/sshd_config, then: sudo systemctl reload ssh, then: ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new grcops@web-01 true, then: ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o BatchMode=yes grcops@web-01 true 2> evidence/ssh-password-refused.txt

tasks.explain:
`Permission denied (publickey).` is the server naming the ONLY method it still
offers. Before the reload that same probe said `(publickey,password)` — the
difference between those two parentheses is the control taking effect, and your
captured refusal is the negative test every auth control deserves.

tasks.instruction:
Evaluate the config the way `sshd` does. First witness the trap: run the naive
`sudo grep PasswordAuthentication /etc/ssh/sshd_config` and notice the commented
decoy in the output. Then resolve the EFFECTIVE value the way the daemon parses it
— comments stripped, last directive wins — keeping only the single effective line
as evidence in `evidence/effective-passwordauth.txt`, and do the same for
`PermitRootLogin` into `evidence/effective-permitrootlogin.txt`.

hints.nudge: Three stages: drop every line whose first non-blank character is `#`, keep only the directive you're resolving, keep only the LAST survivor. The daemon ignores comments and honors the last duplicate — your evidence must too.

hints.concept: §5.3 — evidence must be evaluated by the enforcing program's parse rules, or it's a guess that looks official

hints.reveal: sudo grep -v '^[[:space:]]*#' /etc/ssh/sshd_config | grep -i '^[[:space:]]*PasswordAuthentication' | tail -1 > evidence/effective-passwordauth.txt, then the same pipeline with PermitRootLogin into evidence/effective-permitrootlogin.txt

tasks.explain:
Your evidence file holds exactly one line — the directive `sshd` actually enforces —
with the decoy gone. A naive grep would have shipped the commented `yes` to an
auditor as a false finding. Same file, two methods, opposite conclusions: the parse
rules are part of the evidence.

tasks.instruction:
Control 3: the evidence-collector service must be installed, running, AND
persistent. The package is already on the box — install it with
`sudo apt install -y ./evidence-collector_1.0.0_all.deb`, start it, then run
`systemctl status evidence-collector` and READ the `Loaded:` line before you
celebrate: `active (running)` with `disabled` is a control that dies at the next
reboot. Enable it, then capture the final status with
`systemctl status evidence-collector > evidence/service-status.txt`.

hints.nudge: `apt install` puts the unit on disk, `start` makes it run NOW — neither says anything about the next boot. One word in the `Loaded:` line carries the reboot promise.

hints.concept: §4.3 — a service is a program the OS guarantees keeps happening; §5.4 — read BOTH fields, not one

hints.reveal: sudo apt install -y ./evidence-collector_1.0.0_all.deb, then: sudo systemctl start evidence-collector, then: sudo systemctl enable evidence-collector, then: systemctl status evidence-collector > evidence/service-status.txt

tasks.explain:
Your captured status shows both words that matter: `active (running)` — it is up
now — and `enabled` — it returns after a reboot. A check that records only the
first is a point-in-time snapshot wearing a continuous control's name tag.

tasks.instruction:
In one sentence: if you had skipped `enable`, what exactly would a reviewer find
after the next reboot — and why does a point-in-time "it's running" check miss
that failure mode entirely?

hints.nudge: Think about WHEN each of the two status fields is allowed to become false.

hints.concept: §4.3 / §5.4 — active vs enabled is now vs next-boot

tasks.instruction:
Controls leave records. Query the SSH unit's journal for the login you performed
and keep the proof:
`sudo journalctl -u ssh --since "2026-05-27" | grep -i "accepted" > evidence/auth-event.txt`.
Read your captured line: method `publickey`, account `grcops` — and note that no
successful `password` line exists to be found.

hints.nudge: The journal is queried per unit (`-u`). Which unit witnessed your login — and whose journal do you need sudo to read in full?

hints.concept: §4.7 — /etc is where a control is declared; the journal is where it is witnessed actually working

tasks.explain:
`Accepted publickey for grcops` is the host's own append-only memory of the control
being exercised — not configured, exercised. The absence of any `Accepted password`
line is the other half of the proof, and absence is only evidence when you looked
for the thing and can show how you looked.

tasks.instruction:
Assemble the writeup a reviewer could re-run. Create `evidence-writeup.md` in your
home directory — open the editor with `nano evidence-writeup.md` (or compose it
with a heredoc) — with one block per control: the control statement, WHERE its
truth lives on the host, the exact command, the evidence line, and a final line
reading `Verdict: PASS`.

hints.nudge: Three controls, three blocks. Each block answers four questions: what was claimed, where does its truth live (§4.1), what command was run, what line came back — then the verdict.

hints.concept: §6 deliverable — evidence is defensible when a reviewer re-running every command reaches the identical verdict

hints.reveal: nano evidence-writeup.md — one block per control with its claim, its home (/etc/group · /etc/ssh/sshd_config · the unit + journal), the exact command (id grcops · the grep -v pipeline · systemctl status evidence-collector), the evidence line (27(sudo) · PasswordAuthentication no · active (running) plus enabled · Accepted publickey for grcops) and a final line Verdict: PASS

tasks.explain:
This page is the assessment artifact in miniature: every verdict is welded to the
command that produced it and the line it produced. Anyone with access to web-01 can
re-run your three commands and arrive at your three verdicts — that re-runnability
is what separates compliance evidence from compliance theater.

tasks.instruction:
In 4–6 sentences for a non-technical reviewer: for each of the three controls, name
where its truth physically lives on the host (a declaration in /etc, a record in
the journal, or running state) and how you would find it on an unfamiliar machine.
Then decode `-rw-r----- root root` on /etc/ssh/sshd_config — who can read it, who
can write it, and why that shape is right for a security-relevant config.

hints.nudge: The §3 map: files persist (declarations), processes run, systemd supervises, the journal remembers. Every control is a checkable fact in exactly one of those places.

hints.concept: §4.1 — the filesystem hierarchy is a map of where evidence is kept

# web-01 baseline sshd_config - managed snapshot recorded by GRC ops during host provisioning ..
# This is the sshd server system-wide configuration file.  See
# sshd_config(5) for more information.

# The strategy used for options in the default sshd_config shipped with
# OpenSSH is to specify options with their default value where
# possible, but leave them commented.  Uncommented options override the
# default value.

Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf

#Port 22
#AddressFamily any
#ListenAddress 0.0.0.0
#ListenAddress ::

#HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key
#HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ecdsa_key
#HostKey /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key

# Ciphers and keying
#RekeyLimit default none

# Logging
#SyslogFacility AUTH
#LogLevel INFO

# Authentication:

#LoginGraceTime 2m
#PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
#StrictModes yes
#MaxAuthTries 6
#MaxSessions 10

#PubkeyAuthentication yes

# Expect .ssh/authorized_keys2 to be disregarded by default in future.
#AuthorizedKeysFile	.ssh/authorized_keys .ssh/authorized_keys2

#AuthorizedPrincipalsFile none

#AuthorizedKeysCommand none
#AuthorizedKeysCommandUser nobody

# For this to work you will also need host keys in /etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts
#HostbasedAuthentication no
# Change to yes if you don't trust ~/.ssh/known_hosts for
# HostbasedAuthentication
#IgnoreUserKnownHosts no
# Don't read the user's ~/.rhosts and ~/.shosts files
#IgnoreRhosts yes

# To disable tunneled clear text passwords, change to no here!
#PasswordAuthentication yes
#PermitEmptyPasswords no

# Change to yes to enable challenge-response passwords (beware issues with
# some PAM modules and threads)
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no

# Kerberos options
#KerberosAuthentication no
#KerberosOrLocalPasswd yes
#KerberosTicketCleanup yes
#KerberosGetAFSToken no

# GSSAPI options
#GSSAPIAuthentication no
#GSSAPICleanupCredentials yes
#GSSAPIStrictAcceptorCheck yes
#GSSAPIKeyExchange no

# Set this to 'yes' to enable PAM authentication, account processing,
# and session processing. If this is enabled, PAM authentication will
# be allowed through the KbdInteractiveAuthentication and
# PasswordAuthentication.  Depending on your PAM configuration,
# PAM authentication via KbdInteractiveAuthentication may bypass
# the setting of "PermitRootLogin prohibit-password".
# If you just want the PAM account and session checks to run without
# PAM authentication, then enable this but set PasswordAuthentication
# and KbdInteractiveAuthentication to 'no'.
UsePAM yes

#AllowAgentForwarding yes
#AllowTcpForwarding yes
#GatewayPorts no
X11Forwarding yes
#X11DisplayOffset 10
#X11UseLocalhost yes
#PermitTTY yes
PrintMotd no
#PrintLastLog yes
#TCPKeepAlive yes
#PermitUserEnvironment no
#Compression delayed
#ClientAliveInterval 0
#ClientAliveCountMax 3
#UseDNS no
#PidFile /run/sshd.pid
#MaxStartups 10:30:100
#PermitTunnel no
#ChrootDirectory none
#VersionAddendum none

# no default banner path
#Banner none

# Allow client to pass locale environment variables
AcceptEnv LANG LC_*

# override default of no subsystems
Subsystem	sftp	/usr/lib/openssh/sftp-server

# Example of overriding settings on a per-user basis
#Match User anoncvs
#	X11Forwarding no
#	AllowTcpForwarding no
#	PermitTTY no
#	ForceCommand cvs server

[Unit]
Description=OpenBSD Secure Shell server
Documentation=man:sshd(8) man:sshd_config(5)
After=network.target auditd.service
ConditionPathExists=!/etc/ssh/sshd_not_to_be_run

[Service]
EnvironmentFile=-/etc/default/ssh
ExecStartPre=/usr/sbin/sshd -t
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/sshd -D $SSHD_OPTS
ExecReload=/usr/sbin/sshd -t
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
KillMode=process
Restart=on-failure
RestartPreventExitStatus=255
Type=notify
RuntimeDirectory=sshd
RuntimeDirectoryMode=0755

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Alias=sshd.service

tools.lab-setup:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Lab provisioning tool (module 02 §6 setup). The fixture bytes are canon-locked to
# modules/02-linux-system-fundamentals/labs/setup.sh — a CI drift check asserts equality.
set -euo pipefail
case "${1:-}" in
  02)
    DEST="$HOME/lab02-fixtures"
    mkdir -p "$DEST"
    cat > "$DEST/sshd_config" <<'CFG'
# Managed sshd_config — host web-01 (evidence snapshot)
Port 22
#PasswordAuthentication yes        ← decoy: commented, MUST be ignored
PermitRootLogin no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
PasswordAuthentication no
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
UsePAM yes
CFG
    cat > "$DEST/id-grcops.txt" <<'IDOUT'
uid=1001(grcops) gid=1001(grcops) groups=1001(grcops),27(sudo)
IDOUT
    cat > "$DEST/id-intern.txt" <<'IDOUT'
uid=1002(intern) gid=1002(intern) groups=1002(intern)
IDOUT
    echo "lab02 fixtures written to $DEST/ (sshd_config, id-grcops.txt, id-intern.txt)"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "usage: lab-setup <module-number>" >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
esac
